_comment: What the causal platform can answer, for the systems that propose shadow studies (devbrain on
the RTX 5090 hub, agentcenter and its Oracle on gx10); see shadow/README.md. Plain words first,
then the exact CausalQuery fields. packages/causal-decision/tests/test_shadow_pack.py fails when
this card names a field, design, refusal, verdict or gate the code does not have, misses one it
does have, or was written against another contract version: re-read the card, then bump
question: Did this action cause that result, and should we take it? The answer is an estimate with an honest interval and a verdict, or a refusal that says what is missing.

inputs.graph: A cause-and-effect sketch in the kernel's syntax: 'Z -> X -> Y; Z -> Y'. 'X <-> Y' is an unmeasured common cause, and 'latent U' declares an unmeasured node. A graph node with no data column is treated as unmeasured.
inputs.data: One table: CSV, Parquet, JSON or JSONL. Over MCP, a data_path under CAUSAL_MCP_DATA_ROOTS; over HTTP (POST /api/v1/analysis/run), the rows themselves.
inputs.query: The causal_core.contract.CausalQuery fields named per design below. Declare segment_by, minimum_worthwhile_effect, direction and risk_class before seeing any answer.
inputs.minimums: AnalysisPolicy defaults: at least 30 rows (min_n) and 10 per arm (min_per_arm); fewer is a LOW_N refusal.

designs.name: Effect from ordinary business data
designs.when: Nobody ran a test; there is historical data on who got the action and what happened.
designs.example: Did the email campaign raise spend? (the email-campaign example)
designs.data_shape: One row per unit: the treatment, the outcome, and a column for every measured graph node that drives both.
designs.how: The kernel identifies the effect from the graph (back-door, front-door, instrumental variable or proximal), estimates it with doubly robust estimators and influence-function intervals, then refutes and triangulates.
designs.trust: Rests on the graph: an unmeasured common cause missing from it biases the answer. The sensitivity checks below say how strong one would have to be.

designs.name: A/B test
designs.when: Units were assigned to the action at random.
designs.example: Does the new checkout convert better? (the checkout-ab-test example)
designs.data_shape: One row per unit: assignment and outcome; pre-treatment covariates sharpen the interval.
designs.how: Randomization identifies the effect; covariates are used only for precision.
designs.trust: Strongest design. A broken traffic split (sample-ratio mismatch) is refused when expected_treated_share is given.

designs.name: A/B test watched while it runs
designs.when: The team wants to look at the test every day and stop as soon as the answer is clear.
designs.example: A checkout test read daily, stopped once it is clearly better or clearly worse.
designs.data_shape: One row per unit with an arrival-order column.
designs.how: An anytime-valid confidence sequence: the interval is valid at every look, so stopping early does not inflate the error rate. A sample-ratio mismatch is refused.
designs.trust: Valid at every look; the interval is about 1.5 times as wide as a single fixed-size read.

designs.name: Test by store, team or region
designs.when: Whole groups were assigned together, but outcomes are measured on finer units.
designs.example: A pricing test where each store is in or out; outcomes are per order.
designs.data_shape: One row per measured unit, with the cluster column; treatment constant within each cluster.
designs.how: Cluster-robust (CR2) intervals, so the interval reflects how many groups there are, not how many rows.
designs.trust: Needs enough clusters; very unequal cluster sizes are refused.

designs.name: On and off by time block
designs.when: One shared system cannot be split by customer, so the action alternates by hour or day.
designs.example: Delivery or marketplace pricing switched on and off by time block.
designs.data_shape: One row per observation: the time block (cluster), time within the block, treatment and outcome.
designs.how: Drops the first `washout` time units of every block, averages each block, and compares blocks (Welch on t(K - 2)). A carryover check makes the result contested when the effect is still moving after the washout.
designs.trust: The carryover check has low power against small carryover, so the washout must come from knowledge of the system.

designs.name: Staged rollout over time
designs.when: The action reached different groups at different times and stayed on.
designs.example: A feature launched country by country over three months.
designs.data_shape: Panel: one row per unit per period; treatment switches on once and stays on.
designs.how: Group-time effects against never-treated (or not-yet-treated) units, unit-clustered intervals, an event study, a pre-trends test, and how far parallel trends may fail before the conclusion changes (breakdown).
designs.trust: Tier C: rests on parallel trends, which data cannot prove. The decision layer caps the verdict at experiment when the breakdown is below 1.

checks.name: For whom does it work?
checks.what: An interval per declared subgroup, a wider family-wise interval for looking at several, and one heterogeneity test before any two are compared. The decision layer blocks act when a declared segment is materially harmed.
checks.example: A discount that helps new customers but makes loyal ones churn (the discount-churn example).

checks.name: How strong a hidden factor would have to be
checks.what: The E-value for every result; Rosenbaum bounds (Gamma*) for back-door designs.
checks.example: Ad spend looks great, but demand may have been rising anyway (the ad-spend-hidden-demand example).

checks.name: Refuses where there is nothing to compare
checks.what: A covariate region where one arm never occurs is refused instead of extrapolated; limited overlap is flagged.
checks.example: Every enterprise client got the new plan, so there is no comparison for them.

checks.name: Which earlier answers a revised graph breaks
checks.what: Graphs are stored as versions; causal_impact (MCP) and /api/v1/models/.../impact say, per recorded decision, whether its estimate still holds.
checks.example: An analyst finds a missing factor: which past answers still stand?

checks.name: Were the verdicts right?
checks.what: A follow-up re-runs a decision's analysis on the later window; the calibration report states a rate only from 10 or more follow-ups, each with a Clopper-Pearson interval, and carries undecidable follow-ups into bounds.
checks.example: A quarterly review of how often act was the right call.

refusals.NON_IDENTIFIABLE: The graph does not let the data answer this; it names what would (a measured confounder, an instrument, an experiment).
refusals.POSITIVITY: Some kind of unit was always (or never) treated, so there is nothing to compare it with.
refusals.LOW_N: Too few rows, or too few in one arm.
refusals.UNAPPROVED_ASSUMPTION: The answer would rest on a graph edge nobody has reviewed.
refusals.CI_TOO_WIDE: The interval is too wide to say anything useful.
refusals.DESIGN_CHECK_FAILED: The design's own check failed: a broken traffic split, everyone treated, treatment varying within a cluster.
refusals.RUNG_MISMATCH: The question asks for something other than the effect of an intervention (an association, or a single unit's counterfactual).
refusals.INVALID_ADJUSTMENT_SET: A user-chosen adjust_for set is not valid in the graph.
refusals.WEAK_INSTRUMENT: The instrument barely moves the treatment.
refusals.NO_ESTIMATOR: The effect is identified, but no estimator here handles that identification formula yet.
refusals.INVALID_INPUT: A column is missing, a value is the wrong type, or a data_path is outside the allowed roots.

verdicts.act: Evidence is strong enough and the risk class allows acting without sign-off.
verdicts.act_with_approval: Evidence supports acting, but a named person must approve.
verdicts.experiment: Unsettled; the verdict carries the experiment that would settle it (units, size, duration, guardrails).
verdicts.refuse: Do not act: the effect is harmful, too small, or cannot be estimated.

not_yet: Finding the graph from data (causal discovery); a person or an expert draws it.
One unit's counterfactual (what would have happened to this customer).
Effects that spill between units (neighbouring stores, friends).
Searching for the subgroups an effect differs across; only declared segments are tested.
DiD with anticipation windows, repeated cross-sections or time-varying covariates.
Drift monitoring and plan simulation: promised in docs, not built.
